ai.definition: Precision OncoLogic is an AI platform that integrates advanced artificial intelligence with genomic analysis to develop personalized treatment plans for cancer patients.
ai.howItWorks: The platform analyzes patient data, including genetic markers, to identify the most effective treatments tailored to individual patient profiles.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the need for more precise and targeted cancer therapies by leveraging AI and genomics to improve treatment outcomes and reduce side effects.
ai.buildProcess: Development involves training machine learning models on large genomic datasets, integrating these with clinical data, and continuously refining algorithms through iterative testing and validation.
ai.costDrivers: High costs associated with genomic sequencing, AI model development, and continuous improvement of the platform's accuracy and efficiency.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in an early stage of development and requires further clinical trials to validate its effectiveness before broader adoption.
ai.regulation: Currently no specific regulations apply; however, future developments will likely require compliance with existing healthcare regulations related to data privacy and treatment efficacy.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the accuracy and robustness of AI models. Ethical concerns revolve around data privacy, potential biases in algorithms, and the equitable access to personalized treatments.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current stage of development and high initial costs; potential for significant long-term benefits if successful.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include integrating more advanced AI techniques, expanding the scope of diseases addressed, and enhancing user interfaces for clinicians and patients.

glossary.def: Specific DNA sequences or genetic variations associated with certain traits or conditions.
A medical model that uses an individual's genetic and other information to tailor treatments for specific diseases or conditions.

subsystems.name: Data integration layer
subsystems.role: assembles a complete picture of each patient from scattered hospital records.

subsystems.name: Genomic analysis pipeline
subsystems.role: reads tumour DNA and RNA to find mutations that drive the cancer.
parts: tumour mutational burden and microsatellite instability calculations

subsystems.name: AI/ML prediction engine
subsystems.role: learns from past patients to forecast which treatment is most likely to work.
parts: supervised learning models for drug response

subsystems.name: Clinical decision support interface
subsystems.role: presents ranked therapy options and the evidence behind them to oncologists.
parts: alerting for off-label or trial options

subsystems.name: Validation and monitoring
subsystems.role: proves the platform works in the real world and catches when it drifts.

buildSteps.title: Collect and curate training data
buildSteps.detail: Gather genomic sequences, treatment histories, and outcomes from thousands of consenting patients, with strict privacy safeguards and bias checks.

buildSteps.title: Build a knowledge base
buildSteps.detail: Link genetic variants to drugs, expected responses, and levels of evidence by mining published literature and clinical guidelines.

buildSteps.title: Train and validate AI models
buildSteps.detail: Use the curated data to train models that predict drug response, then test them on held-out patient groups to avoid overfitting.

buildSteps.title: Design the clinical interface
buildSteps.detail: Create a tool that fits into an oncologist's workflow, showing not just a recommendation but why the model made it.

buildSteps.title: Run prospective trials
buildSteps.detail: Compare patients treated with the platform's guidance against standard care to see if survival or quality of life improves.

buildSteps.title: Obtain regulatory clearance
buildSteps.detail: Submit evidence to regulators such as the FDA or EMA for approval as a medical device or clinical decision support tool.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Roll out to hospitals, track real-world performance, and update models as new genomic knowledge and treatments emerge.

prerequisites.why: reading a tumour's full mutational profile is the starting point for matching it to a therapy.
public efforts like The Cancer Genome Atlas have catalogued many cancer types, but data remain fragmented and skewed toward certain populations.
oncologists need to trust a recommendation, so models must explain which genes and pathways drove the suggestion.
without common formats like FHIR, pulling together hospital records and genomic files is slow and error-prone.
regulators are still developing ways to approve systems that learn and change after deployment.

pathway.milestone: AI tools that classify genetic variants or read pathology slides are used in research and some clinics.
pathway.unlocks: faster, more consistent identification of actionable mutations.

pathway.milestone: Integrated platforms combine genomics, clinical history, and imaging to suggest therapies in pilot studies.
pathway.unlocks: oncologists can compare many treatment options at once with evidence attached.

pathway.milestone: Prospective trials show that AI-guided therapy improves outcomes for specific cancer types, leading to regulatory approval.
pathway.unlocks: routine clinical use for those cancers, with reimbursement from insurers.

pathway.milestone: Continuous-learning systems update as new data arrive, and recommend combination therapies or clinical trials in real time.
pathway.unlocks: truly personalised cancer care that adapts as the tumour evolves.
